stanzas: Che bella cosa è na jurnata ’e sole,
n’aria serena doppo na tempesta!
Pe’ ll’aria fresca pare già na festa...
Che bella cosa na jurnata ’e sole.
Ma n’atu sole cchiù bello, oi ne’,
’o sole mio sta nfronte a te!
’o sole, ’o sole mio
sta nfronte a te, sta nfronte a te!
Luceno ’e llastre d’’a fenesta toia;
’na lavannara canta e se ne vanta
e pe’ tramente torce, spanne e canta,
luceno ’e llastre d’’a fenesta toia.
Ma n’atu sole cchiù bello, oi ne’,
’o sole mio sta nfronte a te!
’o sole, ’o sole mio
sta nfronte a te, sta nfronte a te!
Quanno fa notte e ’o sole se ne scenne,
me vene quasi ’na malincunia;
sotta ’a fenesta toia restarria
quanno fa notte e ’o sole se ne scenne.
Ma n’atu sole cchiù bello, oi ne’,
’o sole mio sta nfronte a te!
’o sole, ’o sole mio
sta nfronte a te, sta nfronte a te!
What a beautiful thing a sunny day is,
the calm air after a storm!
In the fresh air it already feels like a feast...
What a beautiful thing a sunny day is.
But another sun, more beautiful, my dear,
my own sun, is in your face!
The sun, my own sun,
is in your face, is in your face!
The panes of your window shine;
a washerwoman sings and boasts of it,
and while she wrings, hangs out and sings,
the panes of your window shine.
But another sun, more beautiful, my dear,
my own sun, is in your face!
The sun, my own sun,
is in your face, is in your face!
When night falls and the sun goes down,
something like melancholy comes over me;
I would stay beneath your window
when night falls and the sun goes down.
But another sun, more beautiful, my dear,
my own sun, is in your face!
The sun, my own sun,
is in your face, is in your face!

notes: The words are in Neapolitan, not Italian: "'o sole mio" is "my sun", "nfronte a te" "on your face" (literally, on your forehead).

The words are in the public domain in the United States, where they were published before 1930; in Italy the song is protected until about 2042, since a court ruled in 2002 that Alfredo Mazzucchi, who died in 1972, wrote the music with Eduardo di Capua.
